abstract: In this study, Vlasov et al. identify a group of enhancer RNAs (eRNAs) that contain open reading frames (ORFs) and are actively translated into stable proteins. Termed eORFs, these eRNA-encoded proteins interact with chromatin and other nuclear complexes (such as those involved in RNA processing and DNA damage response), suggesting that eORFs may function in several nuclear processes.
methods:
Materials and methods
Cell lines
All RNA-seq and plasmid expression experiments were performed in HEK293T cells grown in DMEM containing 10% fetal bovine serum. Cells were passaged by 1 min of treatment with 0.25% trypsin solution at room temperature, with 2–3 day growth periods between passages.
siRNA transfection
For transfection, cells were seeded in 6 well plates. Cells were transfected with siRNA against
Mtr4
or control siRNA against
Renilla
luciferase (siMtr4 and siRLuc, respectively). Cells were grown for 72 h after transfection. For experiments requiring larger cell numbers, such as ribosome profiling, cells were transferred from 6 well plates to 10 cm dishes 24 h after transfection (three wells per dish for siMtr4 transfected and two wells per dish for siRLuc) and grown for the remaining 48 h.
Potential ORF prediction in enhancer regions
The predicted enhancer regions were obtained from the ENCODE Project Consortium, followed by extraction of intergenic enhancers. Considering that eRNAs are bidirectionally transcribed from the center of enhancers and typically span ∼2 kb (
Djebali et al. 2012
), we excluded regions where the central positions were located within 2.5 kb of a gene. ORFs of 300 bp or longer and starting with ATG or CTG were detected using orfipy (
Singh and Wurtele 2021
). Additional coding potential analysis of eRNA ORFs was performed using CPAT (
Wang et al. 2013
). For each protein sequence, we used DEPICTER2 (
Basu et al. 2023
) to predict disordered residues, MoRF (disorder-to-order transition residues), and binding (protein, DNA, and RNA binding). Net charge per residue was estimated using localCIDER (
Holehouse et al. 2017
). All the results were visualized alongside the distribution of amino acids frequently detected in the intrinsically disordered regions.
Lysis and fractionation for ribosome profiling
The ribosome-profiling protocol was based on methods published by Ingolia and colleagues (
Ingolia et al. 2009
,
2012
,
2014
;
Ingolia 2016
) and modifications for footprinting lower-expression genes (
Couvillion and Churchman 2017
). Following 72 h of transfection with siMtr4 or siRLuc, cells were washed twice with PBS and scraped with 500 µL of polysome lysis buffer. Resuspended cells were disrupted with a Dounce homogenizer and centrifuged at 3000 rpm for 5 min at 4°C using an Eppendorf 2424 centrifuge to pellet nuclei. Supernatant samples containing cytoplasm were collected, and RNA content was measured using a NanoDrop spectrophotometer. Four-hundred-fifty microliters of each sample was treated with Ambion RNase I (Thermo Fisher), with the amount adjusted based on RNA content, for 30 min at room temperature and then treated with 5 µL of SuperaseIn RNase inhibitor (Thermo Fisher). Samples were snap-frozen with liquid nitrogen and stored at −80°C.
For sucrose gradient fractionation, thawed RNase-treated cytoplasm samples were centrifuged at 14,000 rpm for 5 min at 4°C (Eppendorf 2424) to remove any remaining cellular debris. Sucrose gradients were mixed from 10% and 50% sucrose buffers using the gradient mixer of a Biocomp gradient station. Samples were loaded on gradients and centrifuged at 39,000
g
using a Beckman Coulter Avanti-E ultracentrifuge. After centrifugation, gradients were separated using the Biocomp gradient fractionator to identify the monosome fractions based on absorbance at 260 nm. Monosome fractions were snap-frozen with liquid nitrogen and stored at −80°C for RNA extraction.
Ribosome footprint RNA extraction
RNA was extracted from monosome fractions using TRIzol–chloroform and precipitated with ammonium acetate, isopropanol, and GenElute LPA. Resuspended RNA was treated with DNase I and extracted a second time by the same method. RNA samples were separated using Novex 15% TBE–urea gels. Gels were stained with SYBR Gold, and bands corresponding to 27–34 nt were cut out. Gel fragments were crushed and resuspended in water to extract RNA, and RNA was extracted from the liquid using TRIzol–chloroform. RNA end repair was done using T4 polynucleotide kinase (NEB) in the presence of ATP, and end-repaired RNA was extracted using the RNeasy MinElute cleanup kit with 3.8× vol of ethanol to ensure removal of all ATP from the sample and prevent adapter concatemer formation during library preparation. RNA samples were tested for appropriate footprint length using an Agilent Bioanalyzer 2100, and concentration was measured using a Qubit assay.
RNA-seq library preparation and sequencing
cDNA libraries were prepared using the NEB Next small RNA library preparation kit. After adapter ligation, rRNA sequences were removed using biotinylated RNA oligos and streptavidin beads (produced by IDT; sequences were from
Ingolia et al. 2012
). cDNA libraries were separated from other fragments by Novex 6% TBE PAGE, and fragments of ∼150 nt (total size of footprint with adapters) were cut out and extracted from the gel. Library size and quality were confirmed using a Bioanalyzer 2100, and concentrations were measured using a Qubit assay. Libraries for all samples were pooled for sequencing. Sequencing was performed on an Illumina NextSeq 500/550 machine at the Columbia Genome Center using a 400 million read 1 × 75 bp sequencing kit. Data were collected and converted to FASTQ format using the Illumina BaseSpace service. Sequencing was performed on three replicates per condition (six total; labeled Mtr4KD_1-3 and siCtrl_1-3) and repeated a total of three times.
RNA-seq data analysis
RNA-seq reads were uploaded to the Galaxy Europe server (
The Galaxy Community 2024
) for analysis. Adapter sequences were removed using Cutadapt (
Martin 2011
), and read length and quality were checked using FastQC (
https://www.bioinformatics.babraham.ac.uk/projects/fastqc
). Remaining rRNA reads were removed by aligning reads against human rRNA sequences using Bowtie2 (
Langmead and Salzberg 2012
), with unaligned reads used for further alignment and analysis. Filtered RNA-seq reads were aligned to the human genome hg19 using the HISAT2 splice-aware alignment algorithm (
Kim et al. 2019
). PAS-seq data were obtained from
GSE267857
representing
Mtr4
KD and shRNA control samples (
Soles et al. 2025
). The stranded bigWig files were generated using deepTools (
Ramírez et al. 2016
), and the read coverage was visualized in IGV (
Robinson et al. 2011
). Transcript sequences were assembled from reads using StringTie guided with a transcript database containing the human transcriptome and all predicted eRNA sequences. Read counts from StringTie (
Pertea et al. 2015
) were quantified and compared using DESeq2 (
Love et al. 2014
).
ORFs were identified, and their translation was verified using RiboTricer (
Choudhary et al. 2020
). RiboTricer automatically separated reads by length and compared positions against published CDS sites to generate metagene profiles and calculate P-site offsets. Read lengths with the highest read periodicity values (28, 29, 31, 32, 33, and 34; phase score ≥0.90) across published CDSs were selected for analysis of putative eRNA ORFs. Novel ORFs in sequences labeled as noncoding were identified automatically by RiboTricer, and those with a minimum of three codons occupied by reads and periodicity matching the minimum for human ORFs (phase score 0.44) were labeled as coding. eRNA ORFs meeting these requirements in at least one
Mtr4
KD sample were selected for further comparison. Putative eRNA ORFs with a significant increase of twofold or greater in read numbers after
Mtr4
knockdown, as calculated by DESeq2 (across all three
Mtr4
KD vs. all three siCtrl samples), and passing the read periodicity test in RiboTricer were identified as likely coding, and the largest ORFs in this group were selected for characterization.
eORFs were compared with OpenProt novel ORFs using BEDTools intersect (
Quinlan and Hall 2010
) and BLAST
+
(
Camacho et al. 2009
) on the Galaxy Europe server. OpenProt annotations were downloaded in BED and protein FASTA formats from
https://www.openprot.org/downloads
. Protein sequences were also searched against a custom BLAST database built from the OpenProt protein FASTA using BLAST
+
protein mode. For eORFs with multiple matches, the largest complete match was reported.
Real-time quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR)
All RT-qPCR reactions were performed using Applied Biosystems Power SYBR Green PCR master mix on an Applied Biosystems StepOne Plus machine. All template cDNA samples were made using Maxima RT reverse transcriptase from whole-cell RNA samples primed with oligo(dT). The results shown in
Supplemental Figure S2
were obtained with two repeats of each sample (control and knockdown) using RPL13a as a housekeeping gene control. Relative quantification values were calculated from threshold cycle values normalized to the housekeeping gene, with log
2
(RQ) equal to the difference of normalized
Ct
values.
eRNA ORF sequence evolution analysis
ORF sequences selected for protein characterization were analyzed for their sequence similarity to homologous sequences in related species. Homologous sequences were identified using NCBI BLASTN search against all recent genomes in the database. For sequences where homologous ORFs exhibited a different length than the human version (typically shorter in other species), only the coding sequence was selected for further analysis. Homologous sequences were aligned using the MAFFT algorithm in the GUIDANCE2 server (
Sela et al. 2015
). Phylogenetic trees for represented species were downloaded in Newick format from the TimeTree server (
Kumar et al. 2022
). kA/kS analysis of sequences was performed using PAML through the CODEML program on the Galaxy Europe server. Visual representations of aligned sequences were obtained using NCBI MSA Viewer and Clustal Omega. The per-residue conservation scores (Jensen–Shannon divergence score) were estimated using score_conservation.py (
Capra and Singh 2007
) using human sequence as a reference, BLOSUM62 as a background, and a Clustal Omega alignment files as an input.
eRNA ORF plasmid design, growth, and expression
Plasmid insert sequences were designed from the largest coding ORFs identified by ribosome profiling. ORFs were tagged with a 5′ His tag and FLAG tag for immunofluorescence and immunoprecipitation experiments. Insert sequences were synthesized and cloned into plasmids through TWIST Bioscience using the pTWIST-CMV plasmid backbone for expression in mammalian cells. Some codon optimization was required for compatibility with TWIST gene synthesis methods, but the amino acid sequences were unchanged. Plasmids were propagated in
Escherichia coli
and extracted using the IBI I-Blue plasmid midi preparation kit. Plasmid sequences and quality were confirmed by sequencing through GENEWIZ.
cDNA amplification was performed using PCR with Phusion DNA polymerase and primers matching the 5′ and 3′ ends of target eORFs, including a C-terminal FLAG and His tag sequence in the 3′ primers. Amplified and tagged eORFs were cloned into a pcDNA3 or p3xFLAG-CMV14 plasmid vector under a CMV promoter; in the latter case, the included 3xFLAG region was not included in the ORF. Additionally, to control for differences in protein expression levels between plasmids, N-terminal tagged constructs were also cloned out of the pTWIST-CMV vector into pcDNA3. Vector control plasmids were the empty pcDNA3 and a pTWIST-CMV containing only the His and FLAG tag sequences under the CMV promoter.
Small-scale plasmid transfection in 6 well or 12 well plates was done using Lipofectamine 2000. Transfections were done with 1 µg of plasmid DNA and 4 µL of Lipofectamine 2000 solution per well in 6 well plates or half of each amount, respectively, for 12 well plates. Transfections were done for 24 or 48 h. For larger-scale expression, PEI-MAX was used instead. Cells in 10 cm dishes were transfected with 15 µg of plasmid and 180 µL of PEI-MAX solution.
Immunofluorescent localization of expressed eRNA proteins
HEK293T cells were seeded on gelatin-coated slides in 6 well or 12 well plates for plasmid transfection using Lipofectamine 2000 (Thermo Fisher). Transfected cell slides were collected after 24 or 48 h. Cells were washed with PBS on ice, fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde, permeabilized with 0.1% Triton X-100, and blocked with Pierce Protein-free blocking buffer. Cells were stained with anti-FLAG M2 antibody (Millipore) diluted 1:500 in Pierce blocking buffer for 1 h at room temperature and then stained with antimouse Alexa fluor 488 secondary antibody diluted 1:500 in Pierce blocking buffer for 1 h at room temperature. Stained cell slides were mounted using Abcam DAPI Fluoroshield mounting medium and sealed with transparent nail polish.
Fluorescent imaging was performed using a Zeiss LSM800 confocal microscope with a 63× oil immersion lens, and images were collected using the ZEN Blue software. Images were processed using ImageJ FIJI software.
Immunoprecipitation of expressed proteins for mass spectrometry and SDS-PAGE
HEK293T cells were seeded on 10 cm dishes and transfected with plasmids using PEI-MAX. Four plates were prepared per ORF sample. Twenty-four hours after transfection, cells were scraped with lysis buffer and disrupted by sonication (10 pulses, repeated three times per sample). For RNase-treated samples, cell lysates were treated with RNase A for 45 min at 4°C on a rotator. For RNase-free samples, lysates were rotated for 45 min at 4°C without RNase A. Samples were then centrifuged at 14,000 rpm for 10 min at 4°C in an Eppendorf 2424 centrifuge to clarify the lysates. Anti-DYDDDDK primary antibody (Cell Signaling Technologies) was added to all samples, which were left to rotate overnight at 4°C. The following day, samples were mixed with Pierce Protein A/G magnetic beads, incubated for 3 h at 4°C, and washed to remove unbound protein. FLAG-tagged protein complexes were eluted using 3xFLAG peptide buffer, mixed with equilibrated TALON metal affinity resin (Takara) beads, and incubated overnight at 4°C on a rotator. The following day, samples were washed and aliquoted for either mass spectrometry sample preparation or SDS-PAGE.
Samples for SDS-PAGE were treated with 2× sample buffer containing 10% β-mercaptoethanol directly on the resin beads. Protein expression and immunoprecipitation were confirmed using Western blotting, gels used were Novex 10%–20% Tris-Glycine Plus gradient gels, and proteins were transferred to PVDF membranes using a Trans-Blot Turbo semidry transfer system (Bio-Rad). Membrane sections corresponding to the size range of each protein of interest were cut to be stained and imaged separately but represent the same SDS-PAGE gel and transfer. Membrane sections were stained for FLAG-tagged proteins using mouse anti-FLAG M2 primary antibody and antimouse HRP secondary antibody or other corresponding primary and secondary antibodies for other proteins of interest. Other proteins isolated by IP were detected using Coomassie staining. The same gel format was used as for Western blotting, and gels were stained with Bio-Rad QC colloidal Coomassie stain overnight and destained with water.
Mass spectrometry sample preparation
The TALON resin containing tagged eORF protein co-IP fractions was incubated in 80 µL of buffer (2
M
urea, 50 mM Tris at pH 7.5, 1 mM dithiothreitol, 5 µg/mL trypsin [Promega V511C]) at 1000 rpm for 1 h at 25°C in an Eppendorf Thermomixer C shaker to partially digest the proteins off the resin. The supernatant containing the partially digested proteins was collected, constituting an initial eluate. Two additional 60 µL washes (2
M
urea, 50 mM Tris at pH 7.5) were performed on the resin; the supernatant of each wash was collected and added to the initial eluate to maximize yield. The full eluate was clarified by spinning at 5000
g
(Sorvall Legend Micro 21).
Half of the partially digested proteins were further reduced with 5 mM DTT at 1000 rpm for 30 min at 25°C and then alkylated in the dark with 10 mM iodoacetamide at 1000 rpm for 45 min at 25°C. Samples were then digested with 0.5 µg of trypsin at 700 rpm overnight (18 h) at 25°C and subsequently acidified with formic acid (for a final formic acid concentration of 1% and a sample pH of ≤3). The acidified tryptic peptides then underwent a C18 StageTip cleanup as described previously (
Rappsilber et al. 2007
). Peptides on the C18 column were eluted with 60 µL of 60% acetonitrile/0.2% formic acid and dried in a vacuum concentrator. Following evaporation, the peptides were reconstituted in 13 µL of 3% acetonitrile/0.2% formic acid for injection onto the mass spectrometer for LC-MS/MS analysis.
Data-dependent LC-MS/MS analysis
About 1 µg of total peptides was analyzed on a Waters M-class UPLC using a 15 cm IonOpticks C18 1.7 µm column coupled to a benchtop Thermo Fisher Scientific Orbitrap Q Exactive HF mass spectrometer. Peptides were separated at a flow rate of 400 nL/min with a 90 min gradient, including sample loading and column equilibration times. Data were acquired in data-dependent mode using Xcalibur software; the 12 most intense peaks in each cycle were selected for MS2 analysis. MS1 spectra were measured with a resolution of 120,000, an AGC target of 3 × 10
6
, and a scan range from 300 to 1800
m/z
. MS2 spectra were measured with a resolution of 15,000, an AGC target of 1 × 10
5
, a scan range from 200 to 2000
m/z
, and an isolation window width of 1.6
m/z
.
Raw data were searched against the human proteome (UP000005640) with MaxQuant (v2.6.3.0). To determine protein enrichment within a sample, the parts per million value of a protein's MS1 intensity value was calculated. This was done by dividing a protein's intensity by the sum of all protein intensities in the respective sample and then multiplying the resulting fractional value by 1,000,000. After that, a pseudocount of +1 was applied before the parts per million values were log
2
-transformed. The log
2
values of a sample relative to the log
2
values of a negative control were subsequently used as an indicator for protein enrichment. The “MS/MS count” (a semiquantitative measure of the amount of peptides identified in MS/MS that match a given protein) was also used as a filter for enrichment with a cutoff of “MS/MS count” ≥10. The significant interactor proteins identified by IP-MS in each condition were subjected to gene ontology analysis using clusterProfiler (
Xu et al. 2024
) using org.Hs.eg.db (
https://bioconductor.riken.jp/packages/3.19/data/annotation/html/org.Hs.eg.db.html
) as a reference and using the Gene Ontology Resource (
Ashburner et al. 2000
;
The Gene Ontology Consortium 2023
) GO enrichment analysis tool (
Thomas et al. 2022
) using all proteins detected by IP-MS as a reference.
Analysis of published MS data
Additional MS data analysis was carried out using the same set of tools as the OpenProt project (
Leblanc et al. 2024
). Whole-cell proteomics MS files were obtained from ProteomeXchange data set PXD005123 (
Noormohammadi et al. 2016
). The FASTA library used for this analysis was constructed from the UniProt human protein database, 53 ATG-eORF proteins, and 15 CTG-eORF proteins described previously. Files were analyzed with the SearchGUI MS tool set using the algorithms X!Tandem, MS-GF
+
, OMSSA, and Comet (
Vaudel et al. 2011
;
Barsnes and Vaudel 2018
). Peptides were matched to proteins from the library using PeptideShaker (
Vaudel et al. 2015
), which was also included in SearchGUI. Results for neural progenitor cell samples 1–6 and hESC samples 1–3 (hESC samples 4–6 produced errors during PeptideShaker analysis) are presented in
Table 3
.
Subcellular fractionation
Fractionation was performed using the method described by
Ogami et al. (2017)
. HEK293T cells were seeded in 10 cm dishes and transfected with plasmids using PEI-MAX, with one plate prepared per sample. Twenty-four hours after transfection, cells were washed with PBS on ice and scraped with PBS. Cells were pelleted by centrifugation at 100
g
at 4°C, resuspended in hypotonic swelling buffer, and incubated for 15 min on ice. After swelling, half of the cell suspension was reserved as a whole-cell sample, and the remaining half was treated with NP-40 at 0.1% final concentration. Cell suspensions and detergent were gently mixed by tapping the tubes and then centrifuged at 6000 rpm for 5 min at 4°C (Eppendorf 2424). Supernatants were saved as cytoplasm fractions, and pellets were resuspended in detergent-free swelling buffer and centrifuged again as a wash step. Pellets were resuspended in 50% glycerol buffer and then mixed 1:1 with 2
M
urea nuclear lysis buffer. Samples were pulse-vortexed three times, incubated for 1 min on ice, and centrifuged at 14,000 rpm for 2 min at 4°C (Eppendorf 2424). Supernatants were saved as nuclear-soluble fractions, and pellets were washed once with 1:1 glycerol and nuclear lysis buffer mixture. Pellets were then dissolved in water as chromatin fractions. Samples were run together for SDS-PAGE and Western blotting. Fractionation was tested using GAPDH or tubulin as cytoplasmic markers, U2AF65 as a nuclear-soluble fraction marker, and histone H3 as a chromatin marker. FLAG-tagged proteins were detected using mouse anti-FLAG M2 primary antibody and antimouse HRP secondary antibody.

body:
Enhancers are distal regulatory sequences that play important roles in the expression of many genes across the human genome. These sites are typically marked by unique epigenetic signatures, such as histone H3 lysine 4 monomethylation and lysine 27 acetylation, that distinguish them from promoters and other regulatory sequences. Enhancers can be located within or outside of gene sequences, and their activity varies greatly between different cell types, tissue types, and developmental stages. Part of the process of enhancer activation and interaction with their target genes involves binding of
RNA polymerase II
(
RNAP II
) to the enhancer site (
Kim and Shiekhattar 2015
;
Field and Adelman 2020
;
Barral and Déjardin 2023
).
RNAP II
transcribes a wide variety of RNAs, including both mRNAs and long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs). At enhancer sites,
RNAP II
transcribes a class of lncRNAs called enhancer RNAs (eRNAs), which are typically relatively short and are often transcribed bidirectionally from active enhancers (
De Santa et al. 2010
;
Kim and Shiekhattar 2015
). Although the functions of eRNAs are not fully understood, they have been found to play roles in gene activation through enhancer loop formation, chromatin remodeling, interacting with and recruiting transcription factors, and possibly mediating heterotypic interactions leading to phase separation during promoter activation (
Hsieh et al. 2014
;
Lai and Shiekhattar 2014
;
Arnold et al. 2020
;
Sartorelli and Lauberth 2020
). Additionally, eRNAs have been implicated in disease; for example, eRNA-associated SNPs have been associated with Alzheimer's disease (
Kikuchi et al. 2019
). Furthermore, not only are enhancers able to produce RNAs similar to mRNAs, but some mRNA promoters have been found to exhibit enhancer-like function (
Medina-Rivera et al. 2018
). Conversely, transcription of eRNAs from enhancers shares many properties with transcription from mRNA promoters, including promoter architecture and transcriptional pausing and release (
Core et al. 2014
;
Henriques et al. 2018
).
eRNAs are naturally highly unstable. These and other unstable lncRNAs are typically targeted by the
Mtr4
RNA helicase for degradation by the nuclear exosome complex (
Zinder and Lima 2017
;
Garland and Jensen 2020
). These lncRNAs include, for example, upstream antisense RNAs (uaRNAs) and prematurely terminated RNAs (ptRNAs), which are transcribed at promoter sites by RNAP II. These lncRNA species share similarities with mRNAs; for example, they all undergo 5′ capping, and some are also spliced and 3′ polyadenylated.
Mtr4
is involved in multiple protein complexes that target different lncRNAs for degradation, such as the NEXT and TRAMP complexes (
Lubas et al. 2011
;
Laffleur et al. 2017
;
Ogami et al. 2018
;
Lykke-Andersen et al. 2021
;
Gockert et al. 2022
;
Puno and Lima 2022
;
Rouvière et al. 2022
). Depletion of
Mtr4
or related quality control factors leads to accumulation of these transcripts, which allows them to be exported from the nucleus and in some cases translated (
Fan et al. 2017
;
Ogami and Manley 2017
;
Ogami et al. 2017
;
Silla et al. 2018
;
Ogami and Suzuki 2021
).
Translation of ORFs located outside of canonical mRNAs has been detected across many RNA species. This includes lncRNAs with already known functions, with most studies so far focused on small ORFs <300 nt (
Ingolia et al. 2014
;
Erhard et al. 2018
;
Olexiouk et al. 2018
). For example, a short ORF encoding a peptide expressed during neuronal development has been identified in the well-studied lncRNA
MALAT1
(
Xiao et al. 2024
). Some ORF-containing lncRNAs were found to be differentially expressed during cancer development across multiple unrelated cancer types such as colon and breast cancer, and their products include both tumor-suppressing and oncogenic peptides (
Zhou et al. 2021
;
Della Bella et al. 2022
;
Wen et al. 2024
). For example, a group of lncRNAs was found to be dysregulated in certain cancers, and some translated to produce small antigenic peptides presented on MHC class I protein complexes, acting as antigens for an antitumor immune response (
Barczak et al. 2023
). Notably, though, lncRNA translation is not limited to small ORFs and can occur on RNAs with their own regulatory functions. For example, the nucleolar lncRNA
PAPAS
is transcribed antisense to rRNAs and is involved in modulating rRNA expression through multiple repression mechanisms (
Zhao et al. 2016
,
2018
). However, in humans and other primates, the transcript also encodes a 229 amino acid protein, RIEP, which is involved in nucleolar and mitochondrial heat shock stress responses (
Feng et al. 2023
).
In this study, we investigated the potential translatability of eRNAs globally in human cells. We first identified ORF-containing eRNA transcripts computationally and found a surprisingly large number with ORFs >300 nt. Ribosome profiling following
Mtr4
depletion was used to identify actively translated eRNAs, and those with the largest ORFs were analyzed further. Remarkably, the encoded proteins were almost all extremely basic, highly enriched in arginine residues, and predicted to exhibit mostly nuclear localization. Analysis of mass spectrometry (MS) databases revealed that many of these proteins accumulate endogenously in cells even in the absence of
Mtr4
depletion, whereas exogenous expression confirmed their stability and primarily nuclear localization. Immunoprecipitation followed by MS provided evidence for association of the proteins with DNA- or RNA-interacting protein complexes. Finally, these large ORFs are conserved in primates, though notably several have human-specific C-terminal extensions. Our results not only provide unexpected new insights into functions of eRNAs but also and more broadly suggest the existence of a large reservoir of previously unknown protein-coding sequences that expand the human proteome in ways yet to be established.
Results
Identification of potentially translatable eRNAs
Our previous work and that of others have provided evidence that certain lncRNAs considered to be noncoding do in fact have the potential to be translated. In this study, we wished to examine globally how widespread this potential is among one such class of lncRNAs: eRNAs. To this end, we obtained candidate enhancer sites from the ENCODE Project Consortium (
The ENCODE Project Consortium 2012
) and chose those where poly(A
+
) RNA-seq results indicated bidirectional transcription originating from them (
Djebali et al. 2012
). To avoid potentially misidentifying mRNAs as eRNAs, we selected only intergenic enhancer sites located >2.5 kb away from the nearest gene for further analysis. Based on these criteria, 20,946 putative enhancer sites producing 41,892 possible eRNA transcripts (two per site) were identified. A preliminary test for the presence of ORFs >300 nt was performed using orfipy (
Singh and Wurtele 2021
) with 5161 eRNAs (∼12%) containing at least one long ORF starting with ATG or with 9259 eRNAs (∼22%) when the alternative possible start codon CTG (
Kearse and Wilusz 2017
) was included. Predicted eRNA sequences were further examined for translation potential using the coding potential assessment tool (CPAT) (
Wang et al. 2013
;
Li and Wang 2021
). Out of all eRNAs tested, 753 contained ORFs rated as having a coding potential of ≥50%: ∼15% of all ATG ORF-containing eRNAs or 1.8% of all eRNAs (though see below).
Ribosome profiling of Mtr4-depleted cells provides evidence for eRNA translation
We next investigated whether any of these eRNAs could be translated. To increase the likelihood of detecting these typically unstable, nuclear transcripts undergoing translation in the cytoplasm, we took advantage of our previous findings that knockdown (KD) of
Mtr4
resulted in the stabilization, transport to the cytoplasm, and translation of certain uaRNAs and ptRNAs (
Ogami et al. 2017
). We therefore performed ribosome profiling (
Ingolia et al. 2009
;
Ingolia 2016
) of
Mtr4
-depleted and control HEK293T cells to identify actively translated eRNAs (
Fig. 1
A; see the Materials and Methods for details). This analysis identified 923 total transcripts upregulated by at least twofold after
Mtr4
KD, including 182 transcripts identified as eRNAs (
Fig. 1
B). Other upregulated transcripts included both mRNAs, other lncRNAs such as uaRNAs, and novel transcripts predicted by StringTie (
Supplemental Fig. S1A
). Although published RNAs included both upregulated and downregulated transcripts, all eRNAs that exhibited significant changes were upregulated (
Supplemental Fig. S1B
). DESeq2 plots for principal component analysis and sample-to-sample distance across annotated genes confirmed clustering into groups of KD versus control for the samples tested (
Supplemental Fig. S1C,D
).
Figure 1.
Identification of translated eRNAs by ribosome profiling. (
A
) Ribosome profiling data analysis pipeline. Reads were aligned by HISAT2. Transcripts were assembled using StringTie guided by the human transcriptome database and predicted eRNA sequences. Reads were quantified and compared between
Mtr4
KD and control samples by DESeq2. eRNA ORFs were identified, and their read periodicity was calculated by RiboTricer. (
B
) Summary of transcripts tested by StringTie and DESeq2 analysis of ribosome profiling reads. eRNA sequences predicted from 20,946 predicted enhancer sites were tested alongside all published human transcriptome sequences. eRNAs were selected for further analysis based on the following criteria: upregulation by >2× in
Mtr4
KD samples (from DESeq2), ORF size of >300 nt (from orfipy, CPAT, and RiboTricer), and read periodicity (from RiboTricer). Fifty-three eRNAs met these criteria, and the 10 containing the largest ORFs were selected (ORF1–ORF10). (
C
) IGV plot of ribosome profiling and PAS-seq reads at the site of ORF2 and
FOXCUT
, with RefSeq genes, the enhancer site, and the ORF location shown
below
. Arrows indicate the relevant ribosome profiling and PAS-seq reads, where applicable, for ORF2 (orange) and
FOXCUT
(violet).
We next set out to obtain a high-confidence list of translated eRNAs by examining properties of the polysome-associated eRNAs identified above. Among the eRNA transcripts with ORFs >300 nt, 53 passed the minimum read periodicity (phase score >0.44) calculated by RiboTricer for human ORF sequences (
Choudhary et al. 2020
). Read numbers and phase scores for all of these eRNA ORFs, which we refer to as eORFs, were within the range observed for typical lower-expression-level mRNAs (e.g., those encoding various ZNF proteins) and for ORFs detected in other lncRNAs, such as
MALAT1
(
Xiao et al. 2024
). All 53 of these transcripts lack introns, as judged by examination of corresponding genomic sequences, consistent with the fact that eRNAs are known to lack introns (
Kim et al. 2015
). We note that this list of 53 eORFs is very likely an underestimate of eRNAs with translatable ORFs, as we set a very conservative threshold for filtering, and many eRNAs that are expressed in a tissue-specific/cell type-specific manner may have been missed in our analysis.
The 53 eORFs display additional properties consistent with their active translation and accumulation in cells. Notably, the largest ORFs among these have a high predicted coding potential; for example, >90% for the 10 largest ORFs (
Table 1

eORF-encoded proteins display common features
The 10 longest ORFs from the above 53 transcripts, ranging in size from 792 to 1332 nt, were selected for further detailed characterization. Expression levels of several of the eORF transcripts were confirmed by RT-qPCR, which matched the previous approximately twofold minimum increase in
Mtr4
KD cells (
Supplemental Fig. S2
). As noted above, all 10 have coding potentials >90%, with most being close to 100% (
Table 1
). Notably, among these 10, which we dubbed ORF1–ORF10, ORF4 and ORF8 are found on eRNAs transcribed from the same enhancer but in opposite directions. The others are localized at distinct chromosomal loci throughout the genome (
Table 1
).
We also observed that the enhancer sites from which the eORFs are transcribed are linked to a wide variety of protein-coding genes. Data on the top 10, derived from the Enhancer Feed-Forward Loop (EnhFFL) database (
Kang et al. 2021
), are shown in
Table 1
. One notable example, ORF2, encoding a 435 amino acid protein, is presented as an IGV plot with ribosome footprints and PAS-seq reads coinciding with PAS sequences immediately downstream from the ORF and illustrates both the enhancer site and eORF (
Fig. 1
C). ORF2 is also noteworthy in that it displays a bidirectional transcription pattern with the lncRNA
FOXCUT
(
Fig. 1
C) and derives from an enhancer of the nearby
FOXC1
gene, as shown in multiple enhancer loop databases (
Bai et al. 2020
;
Kang et al. 2021
). Interestingly,
FOXCUT
contains an intron, which is not typical of eRNAs. Remarkably, however, the intron is human-specific, arising from a 4 base insertion and single base change that together create a 5′ splice site that is unique to humans (
Supplemental Fig. S3
). Additionally,
FOXC1
and
FOXCUT
are noteworthy because both are associated with development and cancer, which may indicate a possible role for ORF2 in these processes as well (
Seo et al. 2006
;
Liu et al. 2015
;
Shi et al. 2024
;
Zhang et al. 2025
). Similar IGV plots, ribosome footprints, and PAS-seq reads for three additional eORFs (ORF1, ORF5, and ORF6) are presented in
Supplemental Figure S4A
.
The predicted amino acid sequences of the top eORFs revealed some striking features (
Table 1
). Remarkably, the isoelectric points of the encoded proteins are highly basic, with all 10 displaying pIs >11.5. In keeping with this, these proteins contain an unusually high number of arginine residues: 10%–20% (average of all human proteins is ∼5.53%; calculated from UniProt database). However, in contrast, the eORF proteins have unusually low numbers of lysine residues (only 0.6%–3.2%; average is ∼5.81%), indicating that arginine richness is almost entirely responsible for their basic chemistry. Notably, these properties extend to a large fraction of the 53 high-confidence translated eORFs, with 42 displaying pIs >10 and 40 displaying arginine richness ≥10% (
Supplemental Table S1A
). Additionally, 15 eRNAs were detected containing ORFs initiating with CTG that match all other criteria used for the 53 ATG-initiated eORFs. Among these, 13 displayed pIs >10, 11 displayed arginine richness >10%, and 13 had lysine contents <3% (
Supplemental Table S1B
). These ORF transcripts also displayed evidence of polyadenylation from PAS-seq reads in
Mtr4
KD cells (ORF_CTG3 is shown in
Supplemental Fig. S4B
). In light of these observations, we also examined eORF codon frequencies for the six arginine codons and compared them with the overall frequencies observed across human coding regions. Seven out of the 10 largest eORFs had >70% CGN arginine codons (as opposed to AGA/AGG) versus the average of 59%. More notably, CGC and/or CGG codons were especially common compared with the average, with as high as 47% CGC versus 19% average and 44% CGG versus 21% average (
Supplemental Table S1C
). The possible basis for and significance of these properties of eORFs are discussed below.
We next used computational analyses to predict subcellular localization of the top 10 eORFs. For this, we used DeepLoc 2.1, which predicts protein localization using protein language models trained with proteins with known localizations (
Ødum et al. 2024
). This analysis suggested nuclear or cytoplasmic/nuclear localization for all the proteins, consistent with their chemical features (
Table 1
). Furthermore, DeepLoc 2.1 predicted that all 10 eORF proteins are soluble rather than membrane-bound (see
Supplemental Table S2
). Although these predictions do not provide insight into structure or function, they do provide evidence for similar patterns of subcellular localization, which is examined directly below.
We also examined intrinsic features of the top 10 eORF proteins, such as ordered versus disordered regions and potential to interact with other proteins, DNA, or RNA. For this, we used the DEPICTER2 program, which can predict these and other properties based solely on primary sequence (
Supplemental Fig. S5
;
Basu et al. 2023
). The results predicted significant disordered regions present across the eORFs, ranging from 27% to 67% of the amino acid sequence classified as disordered. In many cases, these disordered regions included molecular recognition features, which are regions predicted to undergo disorder-to-order transition through interactions with other proteins (
Malhis et al. 2016
). These regions constitute up to 34% of the eORF sequences. All the analyzed eORFs were also predicted to have significant protein and RNA binding ability, ranging from 49% to 99% of the residues capable of protein–protein interaction and 9% to 68% RNA binding. Notably, potential DNA-binding residues were almost entirely absent from these proteins, with only 0%–3% coverage (
Supplemental Fig. S5
).
eRNA-encoded proteins are primarily localized to nuclei and appear to be chromatin-associated
We next examined properties of some of the eORF proteins experimentally. We first designed N-terminal His + FLAG-tagged versions of the proteins and cloned the sequences encoding them into pTWIST-CMV expression vectors (
Fig. 2
A). The resultant plasmids were transfected into HEK293T cells, and as a first step, expression was examined by Western blotting (WB) using anti-FLAG antibodies (
Fig. 2
B). All 10 proteins were expressed at readily detectable levels and gave rise to bands of the expected size, though there was some variation in accumulation. For example, ORF2 was detected at lower levels than the others, whereas several (e.g., ORF7) showed decreased accumulation 48 h after transfection compared with 24 h. Also, several appeared as doublets (notably ORF1), suggestive of post-translational modification.

Immunoprecipitation–mass spectrometry provides evidence for eRNA-encoded protein interactions with RNA processing and DNA damage response complexes
Elucidating the functions of these novel eRNA-encoded proteins will be an important but challenging goal. As a first step, we set out to identify potential interacting proteins for each of the 10 eORFs analyzed above. We transfected HEK293T cells with the expression vectors encoding the His–FLAG-tagged derivatives of each protein, prepared cell extracts, and isolated each tagged ORF and associated proteins using two rounds of affinity purification and FLAG-IP followed by TALON beads. All 10 purifications were performed with both RNase-treated and RNase-free extracts to identify any RNA-dependent interactions. Coprecipitated proteins were then identified by MS (see the Materials and Methods for details). Tandem MS results for all samples were compared against nontransfected samples to identify significant interactors, defined as exhibiting twofold or greater signal quantification over the control and ≥10 spectra detection events (
Supplemental Table S3
). Proteins were also compared between RNase-treated and RNase-free groups to identify RNA-independent, RNA-dependent, and as we somewhat unexpectedly found, RNA-blocked interactions.
Our goal in these experiments was to obtain a general overview of proteins interacting with the 10 eORFs that we have characterized but not to obtain at this stage detailed insights into the functional significance of such interactions. For example, given the surprising similarities in the chemical properties and subcellular localization of the proteins, are there also similarities in the interacting proteins? Especially given the predicted ability of the eORFs to interact with RNA (see above), what fraction of interactions are affected by RNase? As one approach, we used gene ontology (GO) analysis of the MS results to define distinct groups of interacting proteins under both RNase-treated and RNase-free conditions (
Supplemental Table S3
). In the absence of RNase, all 10 eRNA-encoded proteins were found to interact with proteins involved in ribosome structure and function. These included cytosolic small and large ribosomal subunit proteins, which were present in all 10 IPs, and others such as pre-rRNA processing proteins and/or mitochondrial ribosomes, which were detected in several IPs (
Fig. 4
;
Supplemental Table S3B,E,H,J
). IPs of ORF2, ORF5, ORF8, and ORF10 all included components of the small subunit processome, and ORF2, ORF8, and ORF10 included other nucleolar proteins. ORF10 also associated with other preribosomal and ribosomal biogenesis proteins, indicating a possible involvement in ribosome processing/assembly. Other RNA-interacting protein complexes were also detected, such as the coding region instability determinant (CRD)-mediated mRNA stability complex. Notably, DNA-interacting protein complexes were also detected, especially those involved in the DNA damage response (DDR) and double-strand break repair (
Fig. 4
;
Supplemental Table S3B,E,H,J
). Other chromatin-interacting proteins, especially histones, were also detected (see also below).

Ribosomal and rRNA-processing proteins were less represented in the RNase-treated samples, indicating that at least some of these interactions were likely RNA-mediated. These included both cytosolic and mitochondrial ribosomal proteins (
Fig. 4
B,D;

Notably, some of these complexes appeared to have increased representation in RNase-treated samples, which is discussed further below. Interactions observed with the CRD-mediated mRNA stability complex were also resistant to RNase treatment, suggesting possible direct interactions with component(s) of this complex (
Supplemental Table S3E,O

Unexpectedly, several interactions were only detected or greatly increased in the RNase-treated IPs. ORF2 showed an especially large change between RNase-treated and untreated conditions, shifting from primarily interacting with rRNA- and mRNA-associated proteins in the RNase-free sample to more with DNA-associated and rRNA processing proteins in the RNase-treated conditions (
Fig. 4

Supplemental Table S3L,R,T

Fig. 4
D;
Supplemental Fig. S8H,J
;
Supplemental Table S3R,T
). Furthermore, all the histones detected in the RNase-free samples above were present in higher abundance in the RNase-treated samples, and others were detected only in the RNase-treated samples. ORF2, ORF4, ORF8, ORF9, and ORF10 RNase-treated IPs also included proteins involved in chromatin binding and/or nucleosome assembly (
Fig. 4
D;
Supplemental Fig. S8H,J
;
Supplemental Table S3L,N,R,S,T
). The possible significance of proteins appearing in IPs only after RNase treatment is discussed below.
Analysis of proteins coimmunoprecipitated with all 10 ORFs by SDS-PAGE and Coomassie staining and/or WB supports the patterns detected by MS. For example, one notable difference was the increased presence of proteins ∼15 kDa in all 10 RNase-treated samples in Coomassie-stained gels (
Supplemental Fig. S9
). This size profile matched that of histones, consistent with their presence in the IP-MS results and confirming one (histone H3) by WB (
Supplemental Fig. S10
). We also verified several other interactions detected by IP-MS by WB. For example, Ku70 was detected in RNase-treated samples by WB, consistent with its greater presence in RNase-treated IP-MS samples (
Supplemental Fig. S10A
). Similarly, HDAC2 was detected only in ORF6 IP-MS samples, which was confirmed by WB (
Supplemental Fig. S10B
). The ribosome biogenesis protein LAS1L was detected in both RNase-treated and RNase-free samples for ORF1 and ORF10, whereas C1QBP, a multifunctional protein involved in mitochondrial function and ribosome biogenesis, was detected in both samples for ORF8 but primarily in the RNase-free samples for ORF1 and ORF10 (
Supplemental Fig. S10C
). These findings were all entirely consistent with IP-MS results.
We described above evidence from the OpenProt database indicating that multiple eORF proteins can accumulate to detectable levels in cells. These data represent a genome-wide search for novel ORFs supported by MS from multiple sources, including numerous co-IPs from the BioPlex database (
Huttlin et al. 2021
) and multiple cancer lines and other cell types also tested by OpenProt (
Supplemental Table S4A
). Interestingly, one of the OpenProt entries (IP_4463835) we found that matches an eORF (ORF8) (
Table 2
;
Supplemental Table S4A
) was detected in an IP-MS of the putative RNA helicase DHX57, which in turn was among the proteins that we detected that coimmunoprecipitated with tagged ORF8. These findings strongly support the physiological significance of the ORF8–DHX57 interaction. DHX57 is an RNA helicase and homolog of DHX29 and DHX36. Although research on DHX57 is limited, it appears to function in translation initiation and control, similar to its homologs (
Bourgeois et al. 2016
;
Chen et al. 2021
;
Fromont-Racine et al. 2024
) and consistent with ORF8 interactions with ribosomal and ribosome-associated proteins (see above). Why additional reciprocal interactions were not detected in the OpenProt database is unclear but could reflect any number of technical and/or biological limitations; for example, sample preparation, the MS method, or data analysis.

eRNA ORFs are conserved among primates with homologs from related species, providing evidence for recent evolution
We next investigated the evolutionary conservation of the eORFs that we characterized. To address this, we compared sequences of ORF1–ORF10 across different species. We extracted likely orthologs for each of these ORFs using NCBI BLASTN against mammalian RefSeq genomes, identified any ORF(s) within each ortholog, and aligned these sequences using the MAFFT algorithm in GUIDANCE2 (
Sela et al. 2015
; see the Materials and Methods for details).
Notably, all 10 eORFs have detectable homologs in other primates, but significant homologies, especially complete ORFs, were not detected outside of primates. ORF4, ORF8, and ORF10 display homology along their entire length across ape and Old-World monkey species and encode proteins of similar length and sequence (
Fig. 5
A,B; alignments of all 10 ORFs are presented in
Fig. 5
or
Supplemental Fig. S11
; ORF4, ORF8, and ORF10 are shown in
Supplemental Fig. S11D,H,J
). For example, and most strikingly, ORF10 amino acid sequence identity ranges from 99.24% with chimpanzees to 91.63% with macaques (
Fig. 5
B). A similar homology pattern was observed for ORF8 across apes and Old-World monkeys and for ORF3 and ORF4 among great apes (
Supplemental Fig. S10C,D,H
). On the low end of ORFs with complete homologs, ORF9 displays 93.43% identity with bonobos and 85.40% identity with gorillas, whereas other primate matches (including chimpanzees, orangutans, and Old-World monkeys) revealed one or more shorter ORF(s) matching only the N-terminal or C-terminal regions (
Supplemental Fig. S11I,J
). Complete ORFs are not common outside of apes, as most other primate homologs contain one or more smaller ORFs matching the human version. Notably, though, these include multiple cases of insertions or deletions that maintain the reading frame, consistent with selection for the complete protein sequence across these species (
Supplemental Fig. S12A,B
).

Multiple other eORFs show an interesting pattern in which the human protein contains a unique C-terminal extension not found in other species. These human ORFs thus match shorter homologous ORFs in other species with similar or identical sequences at their N termini but contain deletions leading to frameshifts that allow extension by using an alternate reading frame not used in the nonhuman species. For example, ape homologs of human ORF2 contain shorter, 384 nt ORFs, whereas the human version contains a 7 bp deletion, leading to a frameshift that creates a C-terminal extension. The nonhuman versions thus encode a 128 amino acid protein that shares a 72 amino acid N-terminal region with its human counterpart, whereas the postframeshift human version is extended to 435 amino acids in total (
Fig. 5
C). Other examples of C-terminal extensions are present in ORF3, ORF6, and ORF7, though their homologs in other species are more varied without a clear single mutation leading to the extended human version (
Supplemental Fig. S11C,F,G
).
Another interesting class of human eORFs arose from what can be considered gene fusion. In such cases, two closely linked ORFs are present in different reading frames in nonhuman primates, with frameshift mutations leading to the longer, fused human-specific ORF. ORF5 is the clearest example of this, with nonhuman N-terminal homologs encoding a 72 amino acid peptide, whereas the human version contains a 1 bp deletion extending the sequence to 321 amino acids with a shared N-terminal region of 56 amino acids. Distinguishing eORFs in this class from those described above, ORF5 homologs from
Homininae
(chimpanzees, bonobos, and gorillas) contain a second complete ORF potentially encoding a 125 amino acid protein that is fully incorporated at the C terminus of the human sequence by the aforementioned frameshift (
Fig. 5
D). ORF1 and ORF9 display similar patterns of ORF fusion, albeit having a larger set of mutations leading to more varied nonhuman ORFs and thus lacking a clear single event responsible for the longer human version (
Supplemental Fig. S11A,I
).
For some eORFs, partial conservation with more distantly related species was also observed. ORF5, for example, displays limited similarities to New-World monkeys and lemurs (
Supplemental Fig S13A
). Although most eORFs do not display matches outside of primates, ORF4, ORF8, and ORF10 display short matches across a wider range of eutherian mammals, though these more distant similarities are fragmentary and do not cover the entire eORF sequence (
Supplemental Fig. S13B
). As noted above, the eRNAs encoding ORF4 and ORF8 are transcribed from the same enhancer site but in opposite directions, and interestingly, both have fragmentary matches across a similarly wide range of mammalian species. For example, ORF4 shows unusually strong conservation in the region near its start codon, which is conserved well enough to possibly encode peptides/proteins with a conserved arginine-rich N-terminal region across many mammalian lineages, though this homology does not go beyond ∼60 amino acids (
Supplemental Fig. S13B
). This may indicate that the enhancer site from which ORF4 and ORF8 are expressed is much older than the others and formed distinct, translatable ORFs from the same start site in multiple mammalian lineages. It is notable that such patterns of ORF fusion/extension are features of de novo gene formation, as we discuss below.
Notably, CTG-initiating eORFs also display similar patterns of homology among apes and Old-World monkeys. ORF CTG1 exhibits the highest such conservation, whereas ORF CTG3 is conserved only among apes (
Supplemental Fig. S11K,M
). ORF CTG2 has a human-specific ORF formed by a frameshift within a shorter version present in other species (
Supplemental Fig. S11L
).
The presence of intact ORFs maintained across multiple species indicates a likely selection for the complete protein (as opposed to nucleotide) sequence. To provide more insight into the evolutionary conservation that we have observed among these ORFs, we examined the aligned eORF sequences for their ratio of synonymous (kS) versus nonsynonymous (kA) mutations using PAML software (
Yang 2007
;
Álvarez-Carretero et al. 2023
). Coding sequences exhibit a higher proportion of synonymous mutations (kA/kS < 1), indicating stabilizing selection of the amino acid sequence. Typically, human protein-coding genes have kA/kS values of ≤0.35, and higher scores are uncommon outside of certain specific gene groups (
Hurst 2002
). We calculated kA/kS ratios within
Homininae
(humans, chimpanzees, bonobos, and gorillas) for the eORFs that we characterized here (
Table 4
). Among the ORFs with full-length matching homologs, ORF10 displayed the strongest evidence of purifying selection, with a kA/kS ratio of 0.28 across its entire sequence. For the ORFs with human-specific extensions and fusions, ORF2 and ORF5 showed evidence of strong purifying selection in their shared 5′ regions. Thus, the 5′ 216 bp region of ORF2, encoding the shared 72 amino acid N-terminal sequence, has a kA/kS ratio of 0.16 (substitutions are indicated in
Supplemental Fig. S12C
), but this strong sequence conservation does not extend to the 3′ 168 bp of the nonhuman ORFs. With ORF5, the 168 bp 5′ region encoding the shared 56 amino acid N-terminal sequence displays a striking kA/kS ratio of 0.0001, but this strong conservation does not extend to the second 375 bp ORF that is incorporated into the fused human ORF. These low kA/kS values are not maintained when testing a wider group of species (e.g., all primates), indicating that these sequences have only been undergoing purifying selection in recent evolutionary history. Other eORFs analyzed in this study lacked the clear purifying selection of the above three examples. It may be that they are under weaker selection that cannot be detected with significance by PAML, which may in turn be influenced by the higher mutation rate typical of enhancer sites (
MacArthur and Brookfield 2004
;
Villar et al. 2015
). However, for the eORFs with low kA/kS values, the sequence conservation that we detected points to a significant and evolving role for the encoded proteins in primates, with novel ORFs undergoing strong sequence conservation characteristic of known coding sequences (
Álvarez-Carretero et al. 2023
).
